newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Market faces data onslaught.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Market faces data onslaught.

text.p: U.S. credit markets face a busy week ahead as players prepare to digest a full plate of key, sensitive economic data, analysts said.

Overall, analysts expect the fresh indicators to show the economy is still growing, but at a slower pace than earlier in the year. Upward inflationary pressures, they added, are also expected to remain mostly tame.
"We expect the indicators to show the economy is doing well, but not as strong as we had it earlier in the year," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.
If Wall Street expectations are confirmed, traders said prices of Treasury securities might break out of their current ranges and rally to new highs.
Chart analysts have pointed to a strong resistance in the area around 6.38-6.40 percent on the 30-year bond yield.
"We have been consolidating for the past few sessions and if the numbers come in fine we might break out of this range," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
In thin trading Friday, the benchmark bond closed up 31/32 at 101-28/32 to yield 6.36 percent, its lowest level since closing at 6.34 percent March 4.
The data deluge will start on Monday, December 2, with the release of the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) business activity index for November.
The survey, seen as one of the most important barometers of manufacturing activity in the U.S., is expected to show the country's industry is moving but not speeding.
"We don't really expect to see a significant move in the NAPM. We might see a small increase, but other (economic) reports don't suggest we're gonna see a real strong number," Thayer said.
In a Reuters poll, U.S. economists forecast the November NAPM at 50.8 up from 50.2 in October.
On Monday, the market will also get in touch with the construction spending report for October.

On the market's agenda for Tuesday, players will find the new home sales report and leading indicators for October. In a Reuters survey, sales are expected to drop to 772,000 units from 816,000 in September.
"The data will be somewhat important because the housing sector is very interest-rate sensitive," said Marilyn Schaja, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.

On Thursday, players will rely on the initial jobless claims for the week ended November 30 for a fresh insight on the labor market performance. A report on third-quarter nonfarm productivity is also scheduled for release Thursday.
On Friday, the market will chew on the tastiest piece of data for the week: the November employment report.
In a Reuters survey, economists expect non-farm payrolls to have risen 179,000 versus a gain of 210,000 in October. The unemployment rate is seen unchanged at 5.2 percent.

Although most economists expect the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates unchanged for the rest of the year, analysts said that any surprise weakness in November payrolls could really shake the market.
"I think the market can trade significantly better if we get a very favorable employment report," DLJ's Schaja said.

On Friday, the Federal Reserve added reserves to the banking system via over-the-weekend repurchase agreements when fed funds were traded at 5-3/4 percent, above the central bank's 5-1/4 percent target rate.
